problem: Text-only LLM robot planners struggle to perceive the world, and existing mobile robots (including robot dogs) understand and move but cannot manipulate objects or reason about vague, indirect commands. RT-2-style systems use very large models on fixed manipulators.
motivation: A universal robot needs mobility, manipulation, and common-sense reasoning from natural language, ideally with small models that can run autonomously on-board. The authors combine a fine-tuned 7B LLM planner with a separate frozen VLM in an Inner-Monologue / AutoGen-style dialogue, so planning is decoupled from environment appearance.
key_idea: A fine-tuned Mistral-7B generates next-step robot behavior iteratively and calls a frozen MiniGPT-4-v2 through natural-language steps (describe, question, search view) for perception, running on a Unitree Go1 with a gripper.
insight: Splitting planning (LLM) from perception (frozen VLM) lets the planner generalize across unseen objects, backgrounds and environments without retraining. The two-model inner monologue gives the best reasoning score (62 vs 42 for RT-2 PaLI-X). Symbol understanding is weak (24 vs 79 for RT-2 PaLM-E), which the authors blame on MiniGPT-4-v2 rather than the planner. No ablations were run, so these attributions are asserted, not tested.
method: Step-by-step plan generation: Mistral-7B is prompted with the task plus a history of steps and results, and outputs the next step until it emits FINISH.
Action vocabulary: finite steps GO_TO, TAKE, PUT_IN, TILT, SIT, UP, TURN, SAY, FOLLOW, GIVE_TO_USER, GO_USER, each executed by a robot program that returns success or failure to the history.

Environmental analysis steps: DESCRIBE_VIEW, QUESTION_VIEW and SEARCH_VIEW call MiniGPT-4-v2 (frozen, with [vqa] or [detection] tags) on a panorama stitched from three cameras; results come back as free-form language.
Visual-SLAM grounding: detected bounding boxes get object identifiers such as apple [1] and are converted to 3D positions with Visual-SLAM so the robot can navigate to and manipulate objects.

Fine-tuning data: a custom dataset of full scenarios (system prompt, task, list of steps and outcomes) trained so the model predicts subsequent steps and outcomes, reducing the number of samples needed. Released on HuggingFace.
Hardware: Unitree Go1 with a custom gripper and RGB-D cameras, plus a speech model for voice commands.

setting.backbone: Mistral-7B (fine-tuned) planner + MiniGPT-4-v2 (frozen, BLIP-2 style ViT encoder) for perception
setting.model_size: 7B planner (plus MiniGPT-4-v2; total about 4x smaller than RT-2 PaLI-X 55B)
setting.training_data: Custom CognitiveDog robot-behavior dataset of scenario step/outcome sequences (scale not stated); VLM used without additional training
setting.observation: Stitched panoramic RGB from three cameras (front and sides), RGB-D, Visual-SLAM
setting.action_space: High-level discrete skill commands (GO_TO, TAKE, PUT_IN, TILT, SIT, TURN, FOLLOW, GIVE_TO_USER, etc.) with object-ID arguments

numbers_note: The paper's experiments are on custom real-robot manipulation/instruction benchmarks (RT-2-style generalization and emergent capabilities), not a navigation benchmark, so no canonical-benchmark entries are listed. For reference, Unseen Average was 68.06% (Objects 65.5, Backgrounds 73.9, Environments 64.79); Emergent Average was 55.0% (Symbol 24, Reasoning 62, Human Recognition 54). Results appear only in figure-embedded tables.
results: On more than 130 unseen instructions CognitiveDog averages 68.06% vs 62.0% for RT-2 PaLI-X-55B and PaLM-E-12B, and wins on unseen environments (64.79 vs 48.0 for PaLM-E). On emergent capabilities it averages 55.0%, beating RT-1 (16.3) and RT-2 PaLI-X (38.6) and best on reasoning (62), but is below RT-2 PaLM-E (59.0). Complex multi-step tasks are demonstrated qualitatively only.
limitations: Weak symbol understanding due to MiniGPT-4-v2 limitations; the authors suggest extra VQA training
Evaluation uses custom real-world test sets with no ablations, and complex tasks are only shown qualitatively
Baselines are RT-2 numbers on different setups (adapted instructions, objects, environments), so the comparison is not strictly like-for-like
